name: Mass on a spring over a motion sensor, with and without a drag card
fit: The SHO and damped oscillator as the course's first ODEs (F&F 1.1-1.2, 1.6): position is a sinusoid; with damping it is a sinusoid times a decaying exponential.
materials: Spring + ~200-500 g hanging mass from a ring stand
PASCO or Vernier motion detector on the floor beneath (or phyphox on a phone taped to the mass)
Index card / paper plate taped under the mass for air drag
Projector for the live graph
prediction: I tape a big card to the mass to add air drag. Compared with no card, the time for one oscillation becomes: (A) noticeably longer, (B) noticeably shorter, (C) about the same, while the amplitude dies away.
observe: Period essentially unchanged (shift well under 1%) while the amplitude decays exponentially.
explain: x'' + 2 gamma x' + w0^2 x = 0 gives w = sqrt(w0^2 - gamma^2); for light damping the shift is ~ gamma^2/(2 w0^2), second order in a small number, while the decay e^{-gamma t} is first order.
pitfalls: Card too big = big damping and visible period change; that is fine as a follow-up.
Motion sensors need ~15 cm minimum distance.

name: Square wave (repeated Heaviside step) into an RC circuit on a scope
fit: Step-driven first-order ODE (F&F 1.2 setup, 10.10-10.11 Laplace): V_C = V0 (1 - e^{-t/RC}) after each step.
materials: Function generator (square wave), resistor + capacitor, two-channel scope (or the UT Austin-style RC push-button board)
prediction: The square wave's half-period is 20 times SHORTER than RC. The capacitor voltage looks like: (A) the same square wave, (B) rounded exponential steps, (C) a small triangle wave hovering at half the source amplitude, (D) flat zero.
observe: (C) a small-amplitude triangle wave around V0/2; lengthening the period morphs it into (B) exponential charge/discharge curves.
explain: For t << RC the exponential is linear (Taylor: 1 - e^{-x} ~ x), so each half-cycle is a straight ramp; the average settles at V0/2. Ties the Heaviside solution to the later linear-approximation chapter.
pitfalls: Use a generator offset so the square wave runs 0 to V0, or the mean is 0, not V0/2.

name: Step and impulse response of a mass on a spring: add a weight suddenly; tap it with a hammer
fit: Heaviside step and Dirac delta forcing (F&F 10.10-10.11): Laplace predicts x = (F/k)(1 - cos w t) for a step and x = (J/m w) sin w t for an impulse.
materials: Spring + hanger mass over a motion detector (as in spring-motion-sensor-damping)
A slotted mass to drop onto the hanger (the step)
Small rubber mallet or a ruler flick (the impulse)
prediction: Step: the mass hangs at rest; I suddenly add a weight that would stretch the spring 5 cm more if lowered gently. The lowest point it reaches is: (A) 5 cm below, (B) 10 cm below, (C) 2.5 cm below, (D) it sinks slowly to 5 cm. Impulse: I tap the mass sharply upward from rest. The position graph starts: (A) at a peak (cosine), (B) at equilibrium, rising (sine), (C) with a sudden jump in position.
observe: Step: oscillates between 0 and 10 cm below, about the new equilibrium at 5 cm. Impulse: starts at equilibrium with maximum velocity (sine); no position jump.
explain: Step: X(s) = (F/m)/(s (s^2 + w^2)) -> (F/k)(1 - cos w t), max 2F/k. Impulse: X(s) = (J/m)/(s^2 + w^2) -> (J/(m w)) sin w t; a delta force makes a jump in velocity, not position.
pitfalls: Placing the weight must be a release, not a lowering (hold it just touching, then let go).
A tap with a horizontal component makes the mass swing; tap from directly below.

name: Lissajous figures / phasor on an oscilloscope in XY mode with two signal generators
fit: Second option for Euler's formula (F&F 3.4): x = cos w t on one axis, y = sin w t on the other traces the unit circle, i.e. e^{i w t} drawn live.
materials: Oscilloscope with XY mode (any digital scope), projected via document camera or the scope's USB/screen output
Two function generators, OR one two-channel generator with phase control (much better: the phase is set, not drifting)
BNC cables
prediction: Both channels get sine waves of the SAME frequency and amplitude, one on x and one on y. The trace is: (A) a diagonal line, (B) a circle, (C) an ellipse, (D) it depends on something you haven't told me. Follow-up: I now set the y frequency to exactly twice the x frequency; the trace has how many lobes?
observe: With two separate generators the figure slowly morphs line -> ellipse -> circle -> ellipse -> line (the other diagonal) as the phase drifts; with phase control at 90 deg it is a circle, at 0 deg a line. 2:1 gives a figure-eight (or a parabola-like arc at special phase).
explain: x = cos(w t), y = cos(w t + phi). At phi = -90 deg, (x, y) = (cos w t, sin w t), the point e^{i w t} going around the unit circle; at phi = 0 it is a line, in between an ellipse. So the answer is (D): it depends on the relative phase. Slowly drifting generators are a nice live version of a phase phi(t) changing slowly, which is also the beat picture used in class 21.
pitfalls: Two independent generators are never exactly the same frequency, so the figure will not sit still; either use that (it is the answer to D) or use one dual-channel generator.
Older analog scopes are easier to see; on a digital scope turn on persistence / high-res and set equal V/div on both channels so the circle is round.
Visibility in a 40-seat room needs a projected view.

name: Circular motion vs. SHM: shadow of a peg on a turntable beside a pendulum (or mass on a spring)
fit: Euler's formula (F&F 3.4): the peg is e^{i w t} moving around the complex plane, its shadow is Re e^{i w t} = cos w t, and an SHO is exactly that shadow; a second peg 90 deg ahead shows that multiplying by i is a quarter-turn (3.3).
materials: Any turntable with a steady speed: a record player (33 1/3 or 45 rpm), a variable-speed lab rotator, or PASCO ME-8951 rotating platform + ME-8955 rotational motor drive
Peg on the platter near the rim: a ping-pong ball or golf tee hot-glued / taped on a short dowel (radius r ~ 8-12 cm)
Optional second peg 90 deg ahead of the first (different color) for the multiply-by-i question
Pendulum: string + bob from a ring stand with a boom, hung beside the platter so its shadow lands next to the peg's shadow (geometry in notes)
Point-ish light source well off to the side: LED flashlight, phone flashlight, or an overhead / slide projector
White wall or whiteboard for the shadows
Optional: document camera or phone looking straight DOWN on the platter, shown on the projector (that view is the complex plane)
prediction: Q1: The shadow of the peg and the shadow of the pendulum bob start together. After 20 turns of the platter they will be: (A) still exactly in step, (B) slowly drifting apart, (C) way out of step, the peg's shadow moves at constant speed while the bob slows at the ends. Q2 (the Euler one): Peg B sits 90 deg ahead of peg A on the platter. At the instant A's shadow is at its far-right extreme, B's shadow is: (A) also at the far-right extreme, (B) at the center, (C) at the center but moving the other way from (B) -- i.e. ask 'extreme, center, or opposite extreme', (D) at the far-left extreme. Q3 (if the speed is adjustable): double the turntable speed; the peg's shadow (A) moves twice as far, (B) oscillates twice as often over the same width, (C) both.
observe: The two shadows move together: the peg's shadow slows at the ends and is fastest in the middle, just like the bob, and stays locked for many cycles. Peg B's shadow is at the center, a quarter period away from A's (which way it is moving depends on the rotation sense and which side you view from); doubling the speed doubles the frequency at the same amplitude.
explain: The peg's position is r e^{i w t} in the plane of the platter (F&F 3.4); a shadow keeps one component, r cos w t, which is the SHO solution x'' = -w^2 x. Peg B is r e^{i(w t + pi/2)} = i r e^{i w t}, and its shadow is -r sin w t: multiplying by i rotates by 90 deg, which is why sin and cos are a quarter period apart and why x = A e^{i w t} solves the SHO ODE (3.5). The pendulum only matches because sin theta ~ theta; that small-angle caveat is the hook into class 13.
pitfalls: Tuning: a 1% error in pendulum length is a 0.5% period error, i.e. a quarter-period slip after ~50 turns (about 1.5 min at 33 rpm). Fine for a 1-2 min observe; trim the string by eye if it drifts.
Keep the pendulum amplitude small (r/L <~ 0.2 rad): at 13 deg the pendulum is ~0.3% slow, so a large peg radius on a short pendulum drifts faster.
Release the bob from the peg's extreme-shadow position exactly when the peg passes that point (hold the bob next to the peg, let go as the peg leaves it).
The pendulum must swing in the plane perpendicular to the light so its shadow moves along the wall, same direction as the peg's shadow.
Room needs to be dim enough for the shadows; a phone flashlight at 2-3 m works in a half-lit room. Far light = sharper shadows.
Setup and tuning ~20 min the first time; do it before class.
A cheap record player can stall if the peg is heavy or off-balance; use a ping-pong ball.

name: Two identical pendula released at small and large amplitude (period vs. amplitude; photogate variant)
fit: Linear approximation sin theta ~ theta (F&F 2.1-2.2) and the next Taylor term (2.3-2.5): the small-angle SHO period is amplitude-independent only to first order.
materials: Two identical simple pendula side by side, L ~ 1 m (T ~ 2 s), same bob, hung from one rod or two ring stands with booms
Protractor or a cardboard angle template for 10 deg and 60 deg release
Optional photogate + timer in pendulum mode (PASCO / Vernier) for the quantitative 10 deg vs 20 deg version
Optional rigid-rod pendulum (3A95.32) if you want to go past 90 deg
prediction: Main: Pendulum A is released from 10 deg, pendulum B from 60 deg, at the same instant. After about 7 full swings, B is: (A) exactly in step with A, (B) a little behind, (C) about half a swing behind -- swinging opposite to A, (D) ahead of A. Photogate variant: going from 10 deg to 20 deg changes the period by: (A) nothing, (B) less than 1%, (C) ~5%, (D) ~20%.
observe: Main: B's period is ~7% longer, so after ~7 swings the two are swinging in opposite directions (visible from the back row with no instruments). Photogate: 10 -> 20 deg lengthens T by ~0.6% (about 11 ms on a 2 s period), measurable but small.
explain: theta'' = -(g/L) sin theta. Linearizing (sin theta ~ theta, 2.1) gives T0 = 2 pi sqrt(L/g), independent of amplitude. Keeping the cubic Taylor term gives T ~ T0 (1 + theta0^2/16 + 11 theta0^4/3072 + ...): +0.19% at 10 deg, +0.77% at 20 deg, +7.3% at 60 deg, +18% at 90 deg. So the linear approximation is excellent where the correction is quadratic in a small number and fails where it is not; also explains why the class 12 turntable/pendulum match needs a small amplitude.
pitfalls: Release both at the same instant: one person, two hands, or hold both bobs against a ruler and pull the ruler away.
String pendulum at 60 deg is fine (string stays taut); above ~90 deg it goes slack -- use a rod pendulum for that.
Bobs must not collide: separate the pendula sideways by > 2x bob diameter, swinging in parallel planes.
Photogate variant: the 0.6% effect at 10 vs 20 deg is comparable to timing jitter from a sloppy release; average 5 periods and keep L fixed. The 60-deg race is the robust version.
Setup ~10 min.

name: Two air-track gliders and three springs: normal modes and beats
fit: The two-coupled-oscillator problem (F&F 6.9): the eigenvectors (1,1) and (1,-1) are motions that stay pure, the eigenvalues set their frequencies, and any other start is a superposition (beats).
materials: Air track + blower, two gliders of equal mass, three matched springs (glider-wall, glider-glider, glider-wall), two fixed end posts / bumpers
Alternative without air: PASCO dynamics carts on an aluminum track with three springs (CU Boulder version)
Stopwatch or a phone video to time 10 periods of each mode
prediction: Q1: Pull both gliders the same distance in the SAME direction and release (mode 1); then pull them equal distances in OPPOSITE directions and release (mode 2). The frequency of mode 2 compared with mode 1 is: (A) the same, (B) a little higher, (C) about 1.7 times higher, (D) 3 times higher. Q2: Now pull only glider 1 and release with glider 2 at rest. Eventually: (A) both settle to the same steady amplitude, (B) glider 1 nearly stops while glider 2 swings fully, then back, (C) the motion becomes irregular.
observe: Each mode stays pure for as long as it runs; mode 2 is visibly faster, ratio close to sqrt(3) ~ 1.73 with three equal springs. Starting one glider gives energy trading back and forth, with glider 1 nearly stopping.
explain: m x'' = -K x with K = k [[2, -1], [-1, 2]]. Eigenvalues k and 3k, eigenvectors (1,1) and (1,-1) (6.8), so w1 = sqrt(k/m), w2 = sqrt(3k/m): the frequency ratio is sqrt(eigenvalue ratio), which is why (D) is wrong. Starting at (1,0) = [(1,1) + (1,-1)]/2 runs both modes at once; they dephase and rephase, which is the beating (energy exchange) in Q2. The in-phase mode does not stretch the middle spring at all, which students can see.
pitfalls: Springs must be matched (same k) or the modes are not (1,1) and (1,-1); check by hanging the same mass on each.

With w2/w1 = 1.73 the beat in Q2 is fast and only partial-looking; complete transfer needs weak coupling (soft middle spring). Use a soft middle spring for Q2, or use the coupled-pendula entry for the beats.
Air-track friction is low but springs' own mass and sag shift the ratio a few %; quote 'about 1.7'.
Setup ~15 min; air tracks are loud.

name: Two pendula coupled by a weak spring: normal modes and complete energy exchange
fit: Same eigenvector story as the air track (F&F 6.8-6.9), but with weak coupling so the beats are dramatic: one pendulum stops completely.
materials: Two identical pendula (rods or strings with equal bobs) from a common support
Soft spring (or a rubber band) connecting them partway down; adjustable height changes coupling
Commercial coupled-pendulum sets exist in most demo collections (3A70.27)
prediction: Pull pendulum A aside, hold B at rest, release. After a while: (A) A keeps swinging, B picks up a small wiggle, (B) both end up swinging at half amplitude forever, (C) A comes completely to rest while B swings with the full amplitude, then it reverses, (D) it becomes chaotic. Follow-up: start them swinging together (in phase) -- does any energy transfer?
observe: (C): A stops completely, B swings fully, and it repeats. In-phase start: no transfer at all, the spring never stretches. Out-of-phase start: also no transfer, slightly faster swing.
explain: Normal modes (1,1) at w1 = sqrt(g/L) and (1,-1) at w2 = sqrt(g/L + 2k/m). Start (1,0) = half of each. x_A = cos((w2 - w1)t/2) cos((w1 + w2)t/2): the slow envelope is the beat, and A reaches zero exactly when the modes are half a cycle apart. Raising the spring weakens coupling and lengthens the beat period 2 pi/(w2 - w1).
pitfalls: Pendula must be truly identical (same L and bob) or the transfer is incomplete.
Coupling too strong makes the beat too fast to read; too weak makes it take minutes. Aim for a beat of ~10-20 swings.
Release cleanly, no sideways component.

name: Wilberforce pendulum (bounce <-> twist energy exchange)
fit: Coupled oscillators where the two coordinates are not even the same kind (z and theta): the normal modes are mixtures of bounce and twist (F&F 6.9).
materials: PASCO ME-8091 Wilberforce pendulum (or demo-collection equivalent)
Tall stand / rod (~2 m of clearance)
prediction: I pull the bob straight down and release it -- no twist. A minute from now it will be: (A) still just bouncing, a bit smaller, (B) just twisting, not bouncing at all, (C) bouncing and twisting equally forever, (D) spinning continuously in one direction.
observe: (B): the bounce dies out completely into a pure twist, then returns to a pure bounce, repeating (period ~1 s, exchange every ~10-20 s).
explain: The spring couples stretch to twist. With the two uncoupled frequencies tuned equal (adjust the nuts on the bob), the normal modes are bounce-plus-twist and bounce-minus-twist with slightly split frequencies; a pure-bounce start is their sum, so it beats. Starting in a normal mode (lift AND twist the right way) gives no exchange.
pitfalls: Must be tuned (move the nuts symmetrically; UCSC suggests ~7.5 turns as a start); 10-15 min the first time.
Normal-mode starts are hard to hit by hand; the pure-bounce start is the reliable one.

name: Archimedes' volumes by pouring: cone + sphere = cylinder (same radius, height = diameter)
fit: A volume set up as an integral in cylindrical/spherical coordinates (F&F 5.5, 5.7) checked by pouring water.
materials: A clear fillable geometric-solids set with MATCHED dimensions: cone, sphere (or hemisphere), and cylinder of the same radius R and height 2R (hemisphere set: height R). These are common math-education items (fillable 'power solids'); check whether the math department owns one.
Colored water or dry rice/sand, funnel, tray
prediction: Cylinder of radius R and height 2R; a cone and a sphere that fit exactly inside it. Pour the full cone AND the full sphere into the cylinder. The cylinder (A) overflows (B) is filled exactly (C) is filled to about 3/4 (D) is half full.
observe: The cylinder fills exactly: cone (1/3) plus sphere (2/3) of the cylinder.
explain: V_cyl = 2 pi R^3; V_cone = (1/3) pi R^2 (2R) = (2/3) pi R^3; V_sphere = (4/3) pi R^3; these sum to the cylinder. Students then compute the sphere in spherical coordinates (integral of r^2 sin(theta) dr dtheta dphi) and the cone in cylindrical coordinates (F&F 5.5, 5.7), and see Archimedes' slicing argument as an integral over z.
pitfalls: Many students already know 'cone = 1/3 cylinder', so ask about the cone + sphere sum, which few have seen.
Commercial sets are not always dimensionally exact (wall thickness, rounded tips); test that it really fills before claiming 'exactly'.
Water spills; rice is cleaner and shows the same thing.

name: 3D-printed potential surface (or topographic model) with contour lines: release a marble and watch which way it starts
fit: The force is -grad V, perpendicular to the level curves (F&F 8.3-8.4), so 'downhill' means across the contour lines, not along the straight line to the lowest point.
materials: A 3D-printed surface z = f(x,y) with contour lines drawn on it (e.g., the Monroe CC 3D-printed calculus surfaces, STL files free, CC BY-NC), or a 3D-printed relief model of local topography (e.g., the Holyoke Range)
Small marble or ball bearing; overhead document camera
Dry-erase marker for drawing level curves on the print
prediction: The marble is released from rest at point P on the surface; the valley's lowest point is off to the side. In which direction does it START to roll? (A) straight toward the lowest point of the valley (B) along the contour line through P (C) perpendicular to the contour line through P (D) toward the steepest part of the whole surface.
observe: It starts off perpendicular to the local contour line (C), in general not aimed at the global minimum.
explain: The initial acceleration is along -grad V (F&F 8.4), and the gradient is perpendicular to the level curve because V does not change along it, which is why maps put 'downhill' across the contour lines.
pitfalls: Only the INITIAL direction follows -grad V. After that, the marble's inertia carries it off the steepest-descent path (it overshoots and oscillates). Say this explicitly, or students will think the path follows the gradient, which is false for a massive ball; a gradient-flow path would need heavy damping (a ball in honey).
Small prints are hard to see in a big room; use the document camera.
Mostly redundant with equipotential-mapping on the following day; use one or the other as the gradient demo.

name: Electric field / equipotential mapping on conductive paper (Field Mapper Kit), run as a hands-on group activity
fit: The gradient is perpendicular to the level curves and largest where they crowd together (F&F 8.4); students measure a real scalar field V(x,y) and draw grad V from it.
materials: PASCO PK-9023 Field Mapper Kit (conductive carbon paper with a 23 x 30 cm grid, silver conductive-ink pen, corkboard, push pins, leads); about $239. Many intro labs already own it, so ask the lab manager before buying.
One DMM per group, input impedance 10 MOhm or more (any standard digital multimeter), with a banana-to-probe lead
A low-voltage DC source per group: a 6 V lantern battery, 4 x AA, or a bench supply set to 5-10 V
Pre-inked electrode sheets, 3-4 layouts (see notes); the ink needs 20 min to reach full conductivity, so ink them the day before
Colored pencils plus a printed grid template so groups can transfer their points
Optional: the document camera, to show 2-3 groups' maps side by side at the end
pira: 5B20 (equipotential lines/fields in the PIRA electrostatics 5B series; the exact sub-number varies by catalog, so not pinned down)
prediction: Concentric-circle electrodes: inner circle r = 1 cm held at 5 V, outer circle r = 10 cm at 0 V. What does the voltmeter read at r = 5.5 cm, halfway between them? (A) 2.5 V (B) more than 2.5 V (C) less than 2.5 V (D) 0 V, because the field is zero between conductors. Second vote, for the floating-conductor sheet: an isolated metal (inked) ring that is NOT connected to anything sits between the two electrodes. Near and on the ring, do the equipotentials (A) pass straight through as if it were not there (B) bend so the whole ring is one equipotential (C) stop at the ring's edge?
observe: The halfway reading is about 1.3 V, well below half. The equipotentials crowd near the small inner electrode (spacing grows roughly in proportion to r), and the floating ring sits at a single voltage, with the nearby equipotentials bending to wrap around it.
explain: On a sheet the problem is 2D, so V satisfies the 2D Laplace equation and the circularly symmetric solution is logarithmic: V(r) = V0 ln(r2/r)/ln(r2/r1), giving 5 ln(10/5.5)/ln 10 = 1.30 V. It is not 1/r: that is the 3D point charge, and conflating the two is itself a good discussion point (polar vs spherical coordinates, F&F 5.6/5.7). |grad V| = V0/(r ln(r2/r1)) is largest at small r, which is where the contour lines bunch. Groups then draw field lines as curves crossing the equipotentials at right angles, which is the defining property of the gradient (F&F 8.4). A conductor is an equipotential because no current flows along it, and that is why the floating ring forces the contours to bend.
pitfalls: INK DRYING: silver ink needs about 20 min for full conductivity, and the electrode drawing is the step most likely to go wrong. Pre-ink and test every sheet the day before.
The meter must be high impedance (10 MOhm or more, which is fine for any DMM); an analog VOM will load the paper.
Students treat the paper as 3D and expect 1/r. That is intended, but say explicitly in the debrief that sheet = 2D = logarithm.

Edge effects: the paper is finite, so the equipotentials near the paper edges meet them at right angles (no current leaves the sheet). Keep the electrodes away from the edges, or present this as a boundary-condition bonus.
Observation day: the instructor talk cap is 15 min, so the setup slide plus the debrief must fit inside it. Each group's sheet carries its own written instructions.
Allow about 5 min per equipotential line per group. 3 lines per sheet is realistic in the time; 5 is not.

Each group must report at least one quantitative check: the concentric group measures V at 3 radii and compares with the log formula; the parallel-bar group checks that V is linear in x. This is the strongest candidate in the range for the active-learning record. name: Vorticity meter (floating paddle wheel / marked cork) in a free (drain) vortex vs. a rigidly rotating tank
fit: Curl is local spin, not 'the flow goes around' (F&F 8.6; Feynman II Ch 3): v ~ 1/r swirls but has zero curl, while rigid rotation has curl 2w everywhere.
materials: Reliable path: the 1961 NCFMF film 'Vorticity' (Ascher Shapiro), which shows a vorticity meter (a small floating cross carrying an arrow) in rigid-body rotation and in a tub with a small central drain. Free on the Internet Archive.

Optional live version: a large round clear tub or a round basin about 40 cm across, with a small drain hole at the center bottom (or a siphon tube), refilled by a tangential jet from a hose so the swirl is steady
Floating vorticity meter: a 2-3 cm plastic cross, or a cork with a toothpick 'arrow', painted so its orientation is visible from the back row; or a floating paddle wheel with one colored vane
For rigid rotation: the same tub on a turntable or lazy Susan, spun steadily for several minutes before class so the water spins up
Overhead document camera or phone pointed down at the tub
prediction: Water circles a central drain, with speed v ~ 1/r (faster near the middle). A small floating cross with an arrow painted on one arm orbits around the drain. As it goes around once, the arrow (A) rotates once in the same sense as the orbit, like the Moon keeping one face to Earth (B) rotates once in the opposite sense (C) keeps pointing the same direction, say toward the door, the whole time (D) spins many times. Then repeat the vote for a tank rotating like a solid body.
observe: In the drain vortex, away from the core, the arrow keeps pointing the same way while it orbits: no spin. In the rigidly rotating tank it turns exactly once per orbit, in the same sense, at the tank's angular velocity w.
explain: For v = (k/r) phi-hat, curl v = (1/r) d(r v_phi)/dr z-hat = 0 for r > 0: the outer side of the cross is pushed more slowly than the inner side, by exactly enough to cancel the turning of the orbit. All the curl is concentrated at the core, which is Feynman's point and why the line integral around the drain is still nonzero (preview of Stokes, F&F 8.10). For rigid rotation v = w x r, curl v = 2w z-hat everywhere, and a small paddle wheel turns at w = |curl v|/2. Flag that factor of 2 explicitly: the paddle wheel measures half the curl.
pitfalls: A live drain vortex is finicky: the core is rotational (viscous), so a cork that drifts into the core DOES spin. Keep the meter in the outer region and make it small compared to its distance from the drain.
Spinning up a tank to true rigid rotation takes minutes (the spin-up time is set by viscosity). If students see it before it is spun up, the result is muddy.
Surface tension and the meniscus pull floats toward the wall, so use a wide tub.
Water on the floor near electronics; keep it on a tray.
Strong recommendation: show the film segment as the 'observe' step, and treat the live tub as optional color if the lab manager can make it reliable in a dry run.

name: Michelson's Harmonic Analyzer (engineerguy video series): a 19th-century gear machine that sums 20 cosines
fit: Fourier synthesis made mechanical (F&F 9.2-9.3), plus the historical origin of the Gibbs-phenomenon discussion.
materials: Projector + audio; YouTube video 2/4 'Synthesis' (and optionally 1/4 'Intro/History')
Free companion book PDF from engineerguy.com, for Michael's prep
prediction: Michelson's machine adds 20 cosine terms with the exact square-wave coefficients. Near each jump of the drawn curve we will see (A) a perfectly sharp corner (B) a smooth rounded corner (C) a small overshoot 'horn' plus ripples (D) a gap.
observe: The pen draws the square wave with ripples and a visible overshoot near the jumps.
explain: Twenty terms of the series still overshoot by about 9% of the jump: the Gibbs phenomenon is not a machine defect. Historically, Michelson's 1898 letter to Nature about the series' behavior near a discontinuity (from his analyzer work) is what prompted Gibbs's analysis. Ties F&F 9.2-9.3 coefficients to a physical sum.
pitfalls: It is a video, not a live demo: cap it at one segment (about 4-6 min) and pause it for the vote right before the pen draws.
Check the exact part of video 2/4 that draws the square wave in advance; I did not timestamp it.
The historical attribution (Michelson letter -> Gibbs) is standard but I did not re-verify it from a primary source; say 'the story goes' if unsure.

name: The missing fundamental: delete the lowest harmonic and the pitch does not move
fit: The period of a sum of harmonics n f0 is 1/f0 even if the n = 1 term is absent (F&F 9.2-9.4: period and fundamental frequency of a Fourier series).
materials: Notebook or PASCO WA-9307: a 220 Hz tone with harmonics 1-6 at equal-ish amplitude
Powered speaker; optional Friture spectrum display so the class SEES the 220 Hz line vanish
prediction: A 220 Hz note is built from harmonics 220, 440, 660, 880, 1100, 1320 Hz. We delete the 220 Hz component entirely (watch it vanish on the spectrum). The pitch you hear (A) jumps up an octave to 440 Hz (B) stays at 220 Hz (C) becomes a chord (D) becomes noise.
observe: Most listeners still hear a 220 Hz pitch (B); the tone just gets thinner. Sweeping f0 with the fundamental removed, the perceived pitch tracks f0.
explain: The remaining sum sum_{n=2..6} sin(2 pi n f0 t) is still periodic with period 1/f0, because 1/f0 is the smallest common period of all the terms; the waveform on the scope repeats every 4.5 ms, not every 2.3 ms. The auditory system extracts the period, not the lowest spectral line. Ties to F&F's point that a Fourier series on period L contains only frequencies that are multiples of 1/L, but need not contain 1/L itself.
pitfalls: Psychoacoustics is not uniform: a minority of listeners report the octave (A), and both answers should be accepted as honest observations. Explain the PERIOD argument, which is the math, rather than claim 'everyone hears 220'.

Low-quality speakers already suppress 220 Hz (they barely reproduce it), which is the real-world hook (phones do not transmit male-voice fundamentals) but can confuse the 'before' tone. Use a decent powered speaker.
Wikipedia notes the older 'ear nonlinearity' explanation was largely ruled out (Licklider 1954); do not teach it as the mechanism.

name: Fourier synthesis: build a square wave from odd harmonics, live on a speaker and a scope
fit: The first Fourier series (F&F 9.2-9.3) heard and seen as it converges, including the Gibbs overshoot at the jump.
materials: Either: PASCO WA-9307 Fourier Synthesizer (440 Hz fundamental plus 8 harmonics, each with amplitude and phase control). It is an old model, probably no longer sold (not verified), but common in stockrooms, so check before buying anything.
Or (free): a Jupyter notebook on jupyterhub.smith.edu that builds sum_{n odd} (4/(n pi)) sin(n w t) for n = 1..N, plots it, and plays it with IPython.display.Audio
Powered speaker with an aux input (laptop speakers are too weak and too band-limited for the low fundamental)
Oscilloscope fed the ELECTRICAL signal (synthesizer output or the laptop line-out), not a microphone; or just the notebook plot projected
Optional: Friture (free real-time spectrum/scope app) on the classroom laptop to show the spectrum growing
prediction: Start with a pure 220 Hz sine. Now add the 3rd harmonic (660 Hz) at 1/3 the amplitude. Does the PITCH you hear (A) jump up to 660 Hz (B) land somewhere between 220 and 660 (C) stay at 220 Hz with a different tone quality (D) split, so you hear two separate notes? Follow-up vote after N = 1, 3, 5, 7, 9: as we keep adding odd harmonics with amplitude 1/n, does the little overshoot spike next to each jump (A) shrink to zero (B) get narrower but stay the same height (C) grow?
observe: The pitch stays 220 Hz and the sound gets brighter and more 'reedy'. The trace squares up, but the overshoot next to each edge stays about 9% of the jump; it only gets narrower.
explain: The sum of sin(wt) and sin(3wt)/3 still has period 2 pi/w, and pitch follows the period, so adding harmonics changes the shape (timbre), not the period. The square wave's coefficients b_n = 4/(n pi) for odd n, 0 for even n, come straight from F&F 9.2-9.3; the even terms vanish by the half-wave symmetry. The persistent overshoot (peak about 1.18 for a +/-1 square wave, i.e. 9% of the jump of 2) is the Gibbs phenomenon: the partial sums converge pointwise but not uniformly near a discontinuity.
pitfalls: Do NOT put a microphone into the scope: the speaker and room have frequency-dependent phase shifts that scramble the shape, even though the ear does not care (see the phase-blind demo).

Laptop audio outputs are AC-coupled, so a low-frequency square wave sent out the headphone jack shows tilt/droop on a scope. Show the notebook plot for the shape and use the speaker only for the sound.
The PASCO unit is fixed at 440 Hz; with 8 harmonics the top one is 3.5 kHz, which is fine.
A square wave at full amplitude is LOUD and harsh. Start the speaker at low volume.
Some students have perfect pitch or musical training and will answer C immediately. Let them explain it to the room rather than going over it again.

name: Live spectrogram of a sung vowel: same pitch, different harmonic weights
fit: A real sound IS a sum of harmonics of one fundamental; the Fourier coefficients (not the frequencies) are what distinguish 'ee' from 'oo' (F&F 9.1-9.3).
materials: Classroom laptop + projector running Friture (free; rolling spectrogram) or the Chrome Music Lab Spectrogram page in a browser (microphone mode)
The laptop's built-in mic is fine; an external USB mic is better in a large room
A volunteer who can hold a steady note (or Michael)
prediction: A singer holds one note and changes the vowel from 'ee' to 'oo' to 'ah' at the same pitch. On the spectrogram, which is evenly spaced horizontal lines, what changes? (A) the line spacing changes (B) the lowest line moves (C) the line spacing and lowest line stay put, but which lines are bright changes (D) nothing visible changes.
observe: The ladder of evenly spaced lines (the harmonics of the sung pitch) stays fixed, while bright bands (formants) slide up and down across the ladder as the vowel changes. Changing the pitch instead spreads or squeezes the ladder.
explain: Pitch = fundamental frequency = line spacing; vowel = the set of Fourier amplitudes |c_n| (vocal-tract resonances boost certain harmonics). It is a direct visual of 'same period, different coefficients' (F&F 9.2), and a whistle (nearly one line) vs. a hum (many lines) makes the sine vs. non-sine contrast.
pitfalls: Room noise and the HVAC hum show up as their own lines; point them out instead of fighting them.
Use a log or mel frequency axis cautiously: on a log axis harmonics are NOT evenly spaced, which undercuts the point. Friture lets you pick linear.
Chrome Music Lab: I could verify the site but not its spectrogram page content (JavaScript-rendered); test microphone permission on the classroom machine before class.

name: Guitar (or sonometer) natural harmonics: touch the string at L/3 and pluck
fit: A sine series on a finite domain, sin(n pi x/L) (F&F 9.4), with a constraint at one point that kills every mode lacking a node there.
materials: Any acoustic guitar (borrow from the music department or a student), or a sonometer / monochord from the stockroom
Optional: the live spectrogram (Friture) so the class sees which harmonics survive
Tape marks at L/2 and L/3 of an open string (measured nut-to-saddle)
prediction: Lightly touch the open low E string at exactly 1/3 of its length (do not press it to the fret) and pluck. The note you hear is (A) the same as the open string (B) one octave up (2x) (C) an octave plus a fifth up (3x) (D) silence, since you are damping it. Bonus vote: pluck the open string exactly at its middle. Which harmonics are missing from the spectrum?
observe: A clear, bell-like tone at 3x the open-string frequency (C). On the spectrogram, only the 3rd, 6th, 9th... lines remain. Plucking at the middle removes the even harmonics (2nd, 4th...).
explain: The string's shape is sum b_n sin(n pi x/L). Touching at x = L/3 forces y(L/3) = 0, damping every mode with sin(n pi/3) != 0 and leaving n = 3, 6, 9,... The pluck-position bonus is the same calculation for the initial condition: a triangle peaked at L/2 has b_n proportional to sin(n pi/2)/n^2, which vanishes for even n (F&F 9.4 finite domain; previews the 11.3 normal modes).
pitfalls: Touch lightly, and lift the finger right after plucking for a cleaner tone; a guitarist volunteer makes this seamless.
An acoustic guitar is quiet in a big room; use a mic + amp or the spectrogram so the back row gets something.
The 'missing even harmonics' bonus is approximate on a real string (finite finger width, stiffness); the spectrogram shows them strongly suppressed, not exactly zero. Say so.

name: Ohm's acoustic law: scramble the harmonic phases of a tone -- the scope trace changes completely, the sound does not
fit: In the complex series c_n e^{i n w t}, |c_n| and arg(c_n) carry different information (F&F 9.5); the ear (approximately) hears only |c_n|.
materials: Same setup as square-wave-synthesis: PASCO WA-9307 (it has phase knobs) or the notebook with a 'randomize phases' button
Powered speaker; projector for the waveform plot
pira: 3C50.10 (same apparatus); UMD catalog codes H5-15 / H5-16
prediction: We keep the square wave's harmonic AMPLITUDES (1, 1/3, 1/5, 1/7, 1/9) but give each harmonic a random phase. The trace no longer looks anything like a square wave. Will it SOUND (A) identical (B) slightly different (C) completely different, like another instrument (D) like noise?
observe: The waveform turns into a spiky, irregular shape, yet the sound is essentially unchanged (A or B; most listeners cannot tell). Toggle back and forth to let the class judge.
explain: In the complex form f(t) = sum c_n e^{i n w t} (F&F 9.5), each c_n has a magnitude and a phase. The shape depends on both; the power in each harmonic (Parseval) depends only on |c_n|^2, and the ear's cochlea is to a good approximation a spectrum analyzer of |c_n|. That is Ohm's (Helmholtz's) acoustic law. It makes concrete why 'the spectrum' usually means |c_n| and why the phase information is something extra.
pitfalls: This is an APPROXIMATE law: with low fundamentals (below about 100 Hz) and many unresolved high harmonics, trained listeners can hear phase changes as a change in 'roughness'. Say so; don't oversell 'identical'. Use a fundamental around 200-500 Hz and only a handful of harmonics (the UMD recipe) for the cleanest result.
Phase must be changed with the sound running continuously, or else the click when audio restarts gives it away; in a notebook, play two pre-rendered 2 s clips back-to-back.
The speaker's own phase response makes any mic'd scope trace meaningless (point of the demo, in a way): plot the computed waveform instead.

name: Heat front on metal bars with thermochromic (liquid-crystal) strips: does the color front move at constant speed?
fit: The heat equation u_t = D u_xx has no characteristic speed; a fixed temperature level spreads as x ~ sqrt(D t) (F&F 11.1-11.2).
materials: Thermal-conductivity bar set with liquid-crystal strips (copper, aluminum, brass, steel; sold by Sargent-Welch and others; UMD I2-29 uses one), or a copper/aluminum bar with a self-adhesive liquid-crystal sheet (e.g., Arbor Scientific liquid crystal sheet) laid along it
Beaker of hot water (below 90 C) or a hot plate
Stopwatch; document camera; tape marks every 2 cm along the bar
Better if available: an IR camera (e.g., a FLIR phone attachment) for a continuous temperature profile
pira: 4C (heat transfer: conduction); UMD catalog code I2-29
prediction: Dip the end of a copper bar in hot water. The color change reaches the 2 cm mark after about 10 s. When does it reach the 4 cm mark? (A) about 20 s (B) about 40 s (C) about 14 s (D) never. Second vote: which metal's front moves fastest, copper or steel, and by about how much?
observe: The front slows down: doubling the distance takes roughly 4x the time, not 2x. Copper is several times faster than steel.
explain: The only length scale that can be made from D and t is sqrt(D t); for a semi-infinite bar whose end is held at T_hot, u depends on x and t only through x/(2 sqrt(D t)), so a fixed color (temperature) sits at x proportional to sqrt(t) (F&F 11.1-11.2). The metal-to-metal ratio of arrival times at a fixed x is the inverse ratio of thermal diffusivities (Cu about 1.1e-4 m^2/s vs. carbon steel about 1.2e-5 m^2/s, so roughly 9x).
pitfalls: UNTESTED quantitatively. The x^2 scaling holds only at early times, before side losses to air and the far end matter, and only if the dipped end stays near water temperature. A dry run must show it before this goes in front of the class. Tier is 'maybe' until then.

Off-the-shelf bar sets use small spot thermometers, not continuous strips, so you get 1-2 arrival times per bar, which is barely enough for the scaling claim. A continuous liquid-crystal sheet or an IR camera is much better.
Hot water: keep it below 90 C (UMD safety note); keep the strips out of the water.
Copper is fast (seconds), steel is slow (minutes): pick the bar that fits the minutes available.

name: Chladni plate: sand on a vibrating plate collects on the nodal lines of 2D normal modes
fit: Separation of variables in 2D gives normal modes with nodal LINES (F&F 11.3-11.4 generalized beyond the 1D string).
materials: Square and/or circular Chladni plate on a mechanical wave driver (e.g., PASCO SF-9324) with a function generator and amplifier, as in the UMass setup; or a violin bow for the classic manual version
Fine dry sand or table salt; a shallow tray/box to catch it
Document camera looking straight down, so the room can see the pattern
prediction: We sprinkle sand on a metal plate and drive it at a resonance. Where does the sand end up? (A) evenly spread (B) piled where the plate moves MOST (C) on lines where the plate does not move at all (D) all thrown off the plate. Follow-up: at a higher resonant frequency, will there be more or fewer sand lines?
observe: Sand is bounced off the moving regions and collects on sharp nodal lines (C); higher resonances give more, finer lines.
explain: Each resonance is a 2D normal mode, a product-like shape whose zero set is a set of nodal curves (for a clamped rectangle, sin(m pi x/a) sin(n pi y/b) gives a grid of lines). More nodes means a higher frequency, just as for the string. The nodal lines are the 2D analog of the string's nodes (F&F 11.3-11.4).
pitfalls: A center-driven Chladni plate has FREE edges (and a fixed center), so its modes are NOT the textbook clamped-edge sin x sin y modes and do not follow simple integer frequency ratios. Present it as '2D normal modes exist and have nodal lines', not as a check of a specific formula.
LOUD high-pitched tones at higher modes; warn the class and keep it short.
Do not exceed the driver's current rating at high frequency (UMass note); sand gets everywhere, so use a tray.
Find and write down the 3-4 best frequencies in a dry run.

name: Melde's string: an elastic cord driven by a mechanical vibrator at f1, 2f1, 3f1 (and at a non-harmonic frequency)
fit: Normal modes of the wave equation, y_n = sin(n pi x/L) cos(w_n t) with w_n = n w_1 (F&F 11.3), seen as discrete resonances.
materials: PASCO SF-9324 Mechanical Wave Driver (or any speaker-coil string vibrator), plus a function generator with amplifier output (PASCO WA-9867 Sine Wave Generator or similar)
Elastic cord or 'bungee' string, about 1-2 m, tied from the driver to a fixed clamp (ring stand weighted with a lead brick or table clamp)
Black backdrop; optional strobe tuned to the drive frequency to freeze the pattern
prediction: We find the fundamental f1 (one loop). Now drive at exactly 3 f1. Counting both ends, how many nodes? (A) 3 (B) 4 (C) 6 (D) the string just shakes a lot with no stationary points. Follow-up: drive at 1.5 f1. What do we see? (A) 1.5 loops (B) a bigger version of the fundamental (C) a small, messy, non-stationary wiggle (D) 2 loops.
observe: At 3 f1, three loops and 4 nodes (including both ends), with large amplitude. At 1.5 f1 the string barely moves and shows no clean pattern; sweeping up, large standing waves appear only near integer multiples of f1.
explain: Separation of variables with y(0) = y(L) = 0 gives only X_n = sin(n pi x/L), and the time ODE then fixes w_n = n pi v/L (F&F 11.3): the allowed frequencies are discrete, the eigenvalues of the spatial problem. Driving between them excites no single mode resonantly. 'Half a loop' is impossible because it would violate the boundary condition at the far end, which is a direct check of the BC logic. A general shape is a superposition of these modes, weighted by Fourier coefficients (9.4).
pitfalls: The driven end is not a perfect node (it moves a few mm); with large driver amplitude the resonant frequencies are not exact integer ratios. Keep the drive amplitude small.
Have the frequencies for n = 1..4 written down from a dry run (the UT Austin notes say to record and date them); sweeping live to find f1 burns minutes.
Strobe: warn the class first (photosensitivity); it is optional and the standing waves are visible without it.
A bungee cord stretched hard has nonlinear tension; tie it at moderate tension.
Setup 10 min; it can stay assembled from an intro-course reservation if the lab manager is coordinating.

name: Tone bursts of shrinking length: the spectrum widens as the burst shortens (time-frequency uncertainty)
fit: The Fourier transform (F&F 9.6): a signal of duration Delta t has spectral width of order 1/Delta t.
materials: Notebook that generates 1 kHz bursts of 1 s, 50 ms, 5 ms, and 1 ms (rectangular or Gaussian envelope), plays each, and plots |FFT| of each beside it
Powered speaker; optional live spectrogram (Friture) for a finger-snap vs whistle contrast
prediction: We play a 1000 Hz tone for 1 s, then for 50 ms, 5 ms, 1 ms. In the spectrum, the peak around 1000 Hz (A) stays the same width (B) gets wider as the burst gets shorter (C) gets narrower as the burst gets shorter (D) moves to a different frequency. Also: will the 1 ms burst still sound like a 1000 Hz pitch?
observe: The peak broadens roughly as 1/Delta t (about 1 kHz wide for the 1 ms burst, comparable to the carrier itself), and the shortest burst sounds like a click with no clear pitch.
explain: A finite-duration tone is the product of a sinusoid and a window; its transform is the window's transform (width ~ 1/Delta t) shifted to the carrier frequency (F&F 9.6). For a Gaussian envelope, Delta t Delta f has its minimum; that is the same mathematics as the quantum uncertainty principle. A pitch needs several cycles: 1 ms = 1 cycle at 1 kHz.
pitfalls: A live spectrogram has its own analysis window (Friture's FFT size), which itself imposes a time-frequency tradeoff and smears short bursts. The static |FFT| plot of each burst in the notebook is the honest display; use the spectrogram only for the qualitative snap-vs-whistle contrast.
Rectangular windows produce sidelobes (sinc) that students may read as 'extra tones'; use a Gaussian or Hann envelope, or name the sidelobes.
Very short bursts are quiet; normalize energy, not peak, or raise the volume for them.
